course.title.note: The course title was given by the team. Malay writes no comma before "dan". The interface (ms.json's preview banner and preview page) may still use the English name; check they agree.

course.description.source: Discover how different communities express their beliefs, identities, work and power through art and architecture. Explore real objects, paintings, homes, streets and heritage traditions in Southeast Asia and around the world, and learn how cultural ideas change and travel.
course.description.back: Explore how various communities express their beliefs, identities, work and power through art and architecture. Study real objects, paintings, houses, streets and heritage traditions in Southeast Asia and around the world, and learn how cultural ideas change and move from one place to another.

sections.0.question.source: How do an object's form, materials and makers connect it to a society?
sections.0.question.back: How do the form, materials and makers of an object connect it with a society?

sections.0.description.source: Study a Japanese print, a Flemish painting, Javanese batik, Vietnamese and Chinese objects, art made for rulers in Egypt and Peru, and a Mughal court album, and see how making, work, exchange and patronage shape what people create.
sections.0.description.back: Study a Japanese print, a Flemish painting, Javanese batik, objects from Vietnam and China, art made for rulers in Egypt and Peru, and a Mughal palace album, and see how making, work, exchange and patronage shape what people create.
sections.0.description.note: "Flemish" is "Flanders" (lukisan Flanders). "Patronage" is "naungan" and "patron" is "penaung" throughout (TERMS.md). "Court" is "istana" here, as in "album istana"; Lesson 5's key word is also "istana".

sections.1.question.source: How do buildings and landscapes express a community's beliefs, authority and everyday life?
sections.1.question.back: How do buildings and landscapes express a community's beliefs, power and everyday life?
sections.1.question.note: "Authority" is "kuasa" here (the section's broad question); Lesson 4's key word is "autoriti".

sections.1.description.source: Explore Toraja houses, Borobudur, Angkor Wat, the trading streets of George Town and Amsterdam, and the Ifugao rice terraces, and see how people organise space around belief, power, work and the land.
sections.1.description.back: Explore Toraja houses, Borobudur, Angkor Wat, the trading streets of George Town and Amsterdam, and the Ifugao terraced rice fields, and see how people arrange space according to belief, power, work and the land.
sections.1.description.note: "Rice terraces" is "sawah bertingkat", the usual Malaysian term (Lesson 10's key word "teres" is for one terrace).

sections.2.title.note: Lessons 11–15 are translated by the other translator: check these words match their lesson titles.

sections.2.question.source: How do images and monuments tell stories, show work and shape what people remember?
sections.2.question.back: How do pictures and monuments tell stories, show work and shape what people remember?

sections.2.description.source: Read Thai Buddhist paintings, French pictures of rural work and a changing modern world, Rodin's monument to Calais, and two paintings of Prince Diponegoro's arrest, and ask who gets to picture history.
sections.2.description.back: Read Buddhist paintings from Thailand, French pictures of work in the countryside and a modern world that is changing, Rodin's monument for Calais, and two paintings of Prince Diponegoro's arrest, and ask who gets the chance to picture history.
sections.2.description.note: "Prince Diponegoro" is "Putera Diponegoro", as in Lessons 11–20 (TERMS.md); Malaysian writing often keeps the Javanese title "Pangeran Diponegoro". "Great Mosque of Djenné" is "Masjid Besar Djenné", as in Lessons 11–20; "Masjid Agung" is the alternative. "Who gets to picture history" is "siapa yang berpeluang menggambarkan sejarah" (who gets the chance to).

sections.3.question.source: How do museums, conservation and living traditions change what a work means?
sections.3.question.back: How do museums, conservation and traditions that are still alive change the meaning of a work?

sections.3.description.source: Follow Buddhist objects into museums, the Great Mosque of Djenné and the yearly work that keeps it standing, blue-and-white ceramics across Asia, and Mexico's Day of the Dead, then tell a fuller story about a work.
sections.3.description.back: Follow Buddhist objects all the way to museums, the Great Mosque of Djenné and the yearly work that makes sure it keeps standing, blue and white ceramics across Asia, and the Day of the Dead in Mexico, then tell a more complete story about a work.
sections.3.description.note: "Day of the Dead" is "Hari Orang Mati" (Día de Muertos); Lessons 16–20's translator may choose differently: check they agree.
